next-season-styles

Three garments a forecast chose, and the pictures made from them.

What to look at first

What the model predicted. From two years of H&M sales it ranked about 2,000 clothing styles by how hard each would sell, per product on sale, over the 13 weeks after 21 September 2020. Its emerging risers, after a human rule that removed intimates and garments that cannot be told apart in a flat photo, were a beige knit sweater, a red dress and a white jersey top.

What was generated from it. For each style an image generator was given several real H&M photos of the style as a guide, plus a sentence naming two design changes (listed under each picture). Each picture is the best of eight tries, chosen by automatic checks and then by a person looking.

How to judge whether it worked. Is each requested change visible, and is the picture still a believable product of its style? A person confirmed the changes on 4 of 4 concepts (three autumn and winter, one summer); 3 pass every automatic check. To find your own category, browse the forecast below.

An image reader was asked, one yes-or-no question per change, whether the garment has it. smolvlm: answers YY (Y = change visible) (pass).

Looks like a real garment (integrity floor)Passed

The closest real reference must be at least as close as 9 in 10 real products of any style are to their own nearest sibling: 0.901 against a global floor of 0.779 (DINOv2). The floor calibrated within this style alone (advisory) is 0.835: pass.

The global floor gates because garment coherence is not a property of one style. It passes every known-good test image and misses one known-malformed one (a sheer-mesh garment); the within-style floor (advisory) catches that one.

Matches the style's attributes (Gate 2)Passed

Two local image readers, shown only the picture, were asked for product type, colour and pattern: florence2 (advisory): 0.57 (pass); smolvlm: 0.57 (pass).

SmolVLM gates; Florence-2 is advisory because its agreement with the API readers was too low to carry a verdict. A reader that sees a brown trim on a beige sweater will say 'brown': a real limit of scoring colour from a single word.

What the measures mean

CLIP and DINOv2 are two pretrained image models that turn a picture into numbers so pictures can be compared; 1.0 means identical. CLIP compares overall look; DINOv2 compares shape and texture. A check passes only if both pass.

A limit here is the 90th percentile of the same measure between real H&M products of that style. The reference base was widened from 4 to 6 photos per style to as many as 25 (the white top has only 19 real articles in the whole catalogue), which cut the uncertainty of these limits by 2 to 4 times.

How each concept traces back to its predicted style

Read each row left to right: what the model forecast, why, which photos guided the picture, what the design brief asked for, and what the picture actually shows.

Beige knit sweater

  1. Forecast

    Predicted 17.8 units per product on sale per week for the 13 weeks after 21 Sep 2020; an emerging riser. Its forecast is 1.59× its recent level.

    "Intensity" means units sold per product on sale, so a style is not ranked highly just for having many products.

  2. Why the model liked it

    Biggest influences, in order: how many products of this style are on sale, then last week's sales level for this style, then the colour.

    These come from an explanation method called SHAP, which shows which inputs pushed this forecast up or down. Persistence (lag_1) dominates.

  3. Guided by

    The generator was shown up to 8 of the best-selling real photos at once, so they set the type of garment and colour without any one photo being copied.

  4. What the brief asked for

    • a high funnel neck collar
    • dark brown contrast rib cuffs and hem

    These were instructions to the generator, written as one plain sentence, not results.

  5. What the picture shows

    Ribbed beige knit sweater, dark-brown funnel neck, dark-brown cuffs and hem.

    Described by looking at the image.

Closing the loop: scoring the pictures with the same forecaster

Predict, generate, then score the generated picture through the same predictor: the picture is matched to the nearest real catalogue style and the model's forecast for that style is looked up. The match is made by image retrieval (CLIP and DINOv2 similarity to each style's real photos), not by asking a small model to name the style. It stays a prototype: the measured accuracy is below.

Autumn/winter pictures are ranked among 1,980 styles forecast from 21 Sep 2020; the summer picture among 3,000 styles from 1 Jun 2020. The index holds each intended style's own reference photos, so an intended-style match is close to circular; a mismatch is the informative case. Against the full catalogue the sweater maps to an orange sibling that is 0.006 more similar than its intended style (third), and the white top to a neighbouring Blouses style (its intended style is fifth, 0.007 behind); the dress and the bikini top match their intended style, the bikini's confidence dropping from high to medium because three orange, yellow and green all-over-pattern tops are near-ties.

Chance for exact style is 0.05% with 1,980 candidates. It does not clearly beat the baseline on the same 40 photos, so it keeps the prototype label; the full-catalogue number is the honest result. The 72.3% earlier figure came from a candidate set of 415 styles and is optimistic for exactly that reason; the 1,980-style rows are the honest numbers.

Confidence label (one photo per style, 1,980 photos): the exact style is first 45% of the time when the label is high (513 photos), 21% for medium (921) and 10% for low (546); within the top 5 it is 67%, 50% and 27%. Near-duplicate articles within a style make these leave-one-out figures optimistic, and the forecast is for the archetype the picture reads as, not for the new design.

Does the model actually work?

Scored on 12 past dates: at each, the model is trained only on dates whose 13-week answers were already known, then forecasts the next 13 weeks, and we compare with what happened.

The honest headline

Hit@3 in top 20 is 0.528 (guessing: 0.011). An earlier version of this page showed 0.722: that run trained on dates whose answers overlapped the test window. Closing the leak lowers it by 0.194 (paired, 0.111 to 0.250). Against the naive baselines the lead holds; against "same as last year" it is a lead on ranking quality (NDCG, Spearman, WMAPE) but not demonstrably on picking the top three.

Did COVID data help? A second model without training rows whose answers touch March to June 2020, scored out of sample on 13 non-COVID dates, was worse on rank correlation and calibration (spearman -0.056 (-0.126 to -0.015); wmape +0.023 (+0.008 to +0.045), without minus with) and no different on top-k. COVID data did not hurt and mildly helped; the second model also has about 40% fewer rows.

A spot-check you can see

The best-ranked style and the style ranked 1,500th, both on one scale: the dark line is what each style actually sold, the coloured line is what the model forecast from earlier data.

Seasonal view

Same forecaster, same selection rules, a different forecast date: summer picks a different garment.

For summer the model was re-run as of 1 June 2020, using only sales whose 13-week outcome was already known by then. Its top emerging style, after the same editorial exclusions (swimwear bottoms are excluded because a flat photo of one cannot be told from underwear; skipped here: #5 Ladieswear · Swimwear bottom · Swimwear · Blue · Stripe (visual-ambiguity exclusion); #9 Ladieswear · Swimwear bottom · Swimwear · Blue · All over pattern (visual-ambiguity exclusion); #11 Ladieswear · Swimwear bottom · Swimwear · Black · All over pattern (visual-ambiguity exclusion)), is Ladieswear · Bikini top · Swimwear · Orange · All over pattern: predicted 37.9 units per product per week for June to August, against 37.9 realised. One style is one data point: the match is encouraging, not a measure of accuracy.

The summer picture: Orange and white all-over print halter bikini top with a plunging front, thick white binding along the edges and a tie at the neck. Automatic gates: FAIL; human check: the requested changes are visible.

What we could not verify

  • Whether the pictures would sell. The forecast is about styles; the pictures are new designs no customer has seen. Nothing here tests demand for the pictures themselves.
  • Demand, as opposed to sales. Everything derives from what was stocked and sold, not what customers wanted. No inventory data was available; a stock-out check finds a lower bound of 3.76% of style-weeks with a stock-out signature.
  • The image readers are small and were checked on few images. Groq's daily limit and Gemini's free quota ran out (Gemini's replacement key authenticates and passes calibration, but no concept could be re-read), so the panel is two small local models, one of them advisory. The yes/no reader for design changes says yes too easily (right about 'no' 58% of the time), so a person made the final call.
  • Automatic integrity is a proxy. Asking a small model whether a garment is coherent caught none of the three known-malformed test images; a global similarity floor gates and passes every known-good image but misses one of the three (sheer mesh); the within-style floor, reported as advisory, catches all three but cannot be met by a design change in a near-identical style. The human check remains necessary.
  • The limits behind the checks still rest on a modest number of real photos: 8 to 25 per style (the white top has 19 in the whole catalogue).
  • The exact top three. The model finds a useful neighbourhood but not the exact order, because the leaders are nearly tied.
Numbers on this page are read from the CSV tables in reports/tables/. The full argument is in WRITEUP.md; how every file was produced is in SUBMISSION_CHECKLIST.md.
